questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

seeded.answer: Clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation include the significant contribution of documentation burden to burnout, particularly among physicians, where it is ranked as the top self-selected contributor at 52%, surpassing patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1]. Additionally, 64% of physicians report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours, averaging 1.2 hours per day, often referred to as "pajama time" [1]. This after-hours work adds to the frustration, as expressed by a physician who noted, "I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed." [2]. Nurses also express concerns about AI-assisted documentation, with 61% being neutral to skeptical about its accuracy and a primary concern being the potential loss of their clinical narrative voice [3]. A nurse from the ICU highlighted this concern, stating, "My notes are how I hand off a patient safely. If a robot writes them and I'm just rubber-stamping, that scares me more than typing." [4].

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

seeded.answer:
Physicians did not trust the ambient scribe's draft notes because of accuracy issues and unclear UI signals. In early usability tests with the v0.1 prototype, medication dosages were missed or garbled in 3 of 5 sessions, which participants said was disqualifying for direct sign-off without review [1]. Additionally, in the same sessions, 4 of 5 participants read every line of AI-generated text before accepting it, showing a lack of trust in the system's reliability [2].

This cautious behavior persisted even when accuracy improved in later versions. For example, in v0.2 (Sep 2025), although errors dropped, physicians still read every line, expressing frustration that the experience did not feel different [3]. The issue was not just accuracy but also the lack of UI that clearly communicated confidence levels and error types. Specifically, clinicians needed distinct signals to differentiate between general uncertainty and clinically critical errors, such as sound-alike medication names [4]. Without these signals, they could not trust the tool to the point of skimming high-confidence content [5].

[HIGH] (accuracy) The scribe correctly captured the chief complaint and HPI in all 5 sessions but missed or garbled medication dosages in 3 of 5 — physicians said this was disqualifying for direct sign-off without review.

sources.excerpt:

[MEDIUM] (workflow fit) The 'start listening' control required a manual click, which physicians said they would likely forget mid-conversation with a patient.

sources.title: The Longitudinal Physician — Ambient Scribe Journey (v0.1 to Post-GA)
sources.excerpt:
v0.1 (Feb 2025) — Skeptical, reads every generated line; medication dosage errors present in 3 of 5 sessions reinforce that caution.
v0.2 (Sep 2025) — Errors drop, but reading behavior doesn't — still reads every line despite the accuracy gain. A frustration plateau: "why doesn't this feel any different?"
GA Candidate (Jan 2026) — Per-line confidence highlighting introduces the first behavior change: begins skimming high-confidence lines for the first time. Relief, tempered by sound-alike medication names still being a known, monitored gap.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the AI's citations?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted the AI to provide inline citations that directly reference specific chart text, not just general section headers. This was identified as a durable requirement during testing of AI-drafted prior authorization justifications, where nurses emphasized the need to see the exact chart text behind each AI suggestion ("show your work") [1]. In response, inline source citations were added to the prior authorization drafting panel, showing the chart entry and date for every claim in the generated justification. These citations were validated as actively used, not ignored, in later testing [2]. The need for inline citations was also highlighted in usability testing of the first version of the AI-assisted prior authorization drafting, where participants stressed the importance of being able to verify the source of each AI-generated claim [3].

questions.question: How did new admins expect the invite step to work?

seeded.answer: New admins were unsure whether invites would send immediately or only after completing the entire setup process. This uncertainty caused hesitation at step 4 ("Invite your team") of the onboarding flow [1]. All three participants in the onboarding study paused at this step with the same concern [2]. For example, in one session, Dana stopped at step 4 and added a test email first to see what would happen, as the current design gave her no safe way to test it [3]. To address this, the design team carried forward an explicit banner stating "Invites will send when you finish setup" and a draft/preview list showing a "not sent yet" state [4]. A wireframe for the reworked step 4 incorporated these changes [5].

questions.question: What haven't we learned yet about care coordinators?

seeded.answer: We haven't learned how care coordinators would use a system that captures the reasoning behind their overrides of alert rankings, which is currently missing in the design [1]. Additionally, we lack insight into how incorporating patient history or continuity signals into the ranking logic might change their behavior or satisfaction, as this was only recommended as a future investigation [1]. There is also no information on how care coordinators would react to a more integrated system that reduces the need for manual cross-referencing of multiple systems, which is currently a high cognitive load task [2]. Finally, we have not explored how care coordinators might interact with a system that provides only change summaries rather than full auto-generated summaries, which they currently distrust [3].

It was faster (6.5 min vs. 9 min to clear a 20-item queue), but 4 of 5 participants disagreed with at least one ranking decision, generally because the model weighted recency over coordinators' own sense of patient-history-driven risk — echoing the alert-fatigue concern raised separately in the May clinician dashboard testing (see [clinician-experience-documentation-burden.md](clinician-experience-documentation-burden.md)). There was also no way to capture why a coordinator overrode a ranking, which both loses a model-improvement signal and undercuts the sense of agency the supervisor specifically flagged as a risk (fast-but-wrong being worse than slow-but-right in this workflow).

questions.question: What is unresolved about the session timeout?

seeded.answer: The unresolved issue about the session timeout is the UI's communication during the idle period, not the timeout policy itself. Specifically, clinicians perceive a session lock during active dictation as silent data loss, even though the draft is preserved server-side [1]. The 10-minute idle timeout policy is fixed and out of scope for change, but the UI does not clearly indicate that the session is paused and the draft is preserved [2]. This lack of clarity leads clinicians to assume they have lost their work and to restart dictation from scratch [1]. IT Security confirmed that while the timeout window is a fixed policy, what the screen communicates during that window is a product decision and can be changed [3]. The UI needs an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state to address this issue [4].
